name: Omega-6 fatty acids
short: Diet trial: linoleic acid for saturated fat raised deaths in men after a heart event; cohorts link more intake to fewer deaths. GLA oils: mild gut effects; primrose oil may raise bleeding on warfarin.
text: Omega-6 fatty acids are a group, and the cited evidence covers two of them separately: linoleic acid, mostly from diet rather than supplements, and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) from evening primrose and borage oil taken by mouth. In recovered data from a randomised trial in 458 men aged 30-59 with a recent coronary event, replacing dietary saturated fat with linoleic acid from safflower oil and margarine increased death rates (all causes 17.6% vs 11.8%; cardiovascular disease 17.2% vs 11.0%), and an updated meta-analysis of linoleic acid trials showed non-significant trends towards more deaths from coronary heart disease and cardiovascular disease. In recovered data from a second randomised trial in 9423 people in a nursing home and mental hospitals, a corn-oil diet rich in linoleic acid lowered cholesterol but showed no mortality benefit, and within the trial, in covariate-adjusted analyses, each 30 mg/dL fall in serum cholesterol was associated with a 22% higher risk of death (an association; the abstract reports cholesterol followed over time in 2355 participants who were on the study diets for a year or more). In contrast, a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies (811,069 participants with diet assessment) found that higher linoleic acid intake was associated with a modestly lower risk of death from all causes, cardiovascular disease and cancer; associations do not show cause. A Cochrane review of omega-6 for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, limited to trials lasting at least six months in healthy adults or adults at high risk of cardiovascular disease, included 4 trials (660 participants) and found no trials of increasing or decreasing omega-6 intake that reported cardiovascular events. For GLA, a Cochrane review of 27 eczema trials (1596 participants) found that evening primrose oil and borage oil taken by mouth had the same fairly common, mild, transient, mainly gastrointestinal adverse effects as placebo; it noted that these short-term trials did not examine long-term use, that a case report warned of a potential risk of inflammation, thrombosis and immunosuppression with evening primrose oil taken for more than a year, and that another study found evening primrose oil may increase bleeding in people taking warfarin.
